name: ossl_ackm_on_rx_packet
prose: Records the receipt of a QUIC packet in the acknowledgement manager. Precondition: ackm and pkt are valid and pkt->pkt_space is a valid packet number space. If the packet number is not processable (already processed or written off, as reported by ossl_ackm_is_rx_pn_processable) it returns 1 without changing anything. Otherwise it updates the largest received packet number and its receive time for that space when the new number is larger, remembers whether the number had been implied missing by an earlier ACK frame, and adds the number to the receive history; if adding fails (rx_pkt_history_add_pn returns something other than 1) it returns 0 (the largest-number update has already been applied). For an ack-eliciting packet it then calls ackm_on_rx_ack_eliciting, which may bring forward the ACK flush deadline (immediately if the number was previously missing, subject to that helper). Finally it increments the ECT0, ECT1 or ECN-CE counter of that space according to pkt->ecn (no counter for other values) and returns 1.

name: ch_rx_handle_packet
prose: Processes the single received QUIC packet held in ch->qrx_pkt and returns nothing. Precondition: ch->qrx_pkt is non-NULL (asserted in debug builds). It returns without effect if the channel is not active, or if the packet is of an encrypted type and its encryption level has already been discarded. For the first encrypted packet it records the remote source connection id as the current remote destination id and initial source id, marks that an encrypted packet was received and tells the packet transmitter. For a client it silently ignores a packet whose source address differs from the current peer address, and a packet that carries a source connection id different from the initial one. A packet with a version that is not QUIC version 1 is dropped. A version negotiation packet (version field 0) is ignored if it is malformed or if any packet was processed before it; otherwise the supported versions in it are scanned and if version 1 is listed the packet transmitter version is set and the channel is restarted with ch_restart (an internal protocol error if that fails), else a connection-refused protocol error (unsupported version) is raised. For other packets it marks that a packet was processed, and an encrypted packet with non-zero reserved header bits raises a protocol violation and is dropped. After logging the packet it dispatches by type: a Retry packet is ignored when the channel is already retrying, is a server, has already received an encrypted packet, is too short, or fails the integrity-tag check, and otherwise is handled with ch_retry (an internal error is raised if that fails); a 0-RTT packet is ignored by a client and otherwise does nothing further here; Initial, Handshake and 1-RTT packets cause a server to discard the initial encryption level when a handshake packet arrives, raise a key-update error for a 1-RTT packet with an old key epoch during a pending key update, raise a protocol violation if a client receives an Initial packet carrying a token, and otherwise pass the packet to ossl_quic_handle_frames (result not checked) and run ch_tick_tls if a crypto frame was seen; any other type is unexpected (assertion).

name: ossl_quic_conn_shutdown
prose: Shuts down a QUIC connection in up to three phases and reports whether it is complete. Precondition: s is a QUIC connection SSL (not a stream); the function takes the connection lock itself, so the caller must not hold it. flags select behaviour (no stream flush, no blocking, wait for the peer, rapid); args may be NULL, otherwise it supplies the application error code and reason. Returns -1 if s is not a QUIC object or is a stream object (the latter raises SSL_R_CONN_USE_ONLY). It returns 1 immediately if the channel is already terminated. Phase 1 (only when not waiting for the peer and stream flushing is wanted): it starts the stream flush and, if not finished, waits for it when blocking is allowed (a failed or interrupted wait ends the call with return 0) or else just ticks the reactor if autotick is enabled; if the flush is still not finished it returns 0 (ongoing). Phase 2 (only with wait-for-peer and the channel not yet terminating): it waits for the peer to close (failed wait returns 0) or ticks, and returns 0 if the channel is still not terminating. It then marks the connection as shutting down, requests a local close with the given error code and reason (a no-op if already terminating), sets the TLS object SSL_SENT_SHUTDOWN, and returns 1 if the channel is now terminated. Phase 3: unless no-block or rapid is set (or the connection is non-blocking) it waits for termination (failed wait returns 0), else it ticks if autotick is enabled; the result is whether the channel is terminated (1) or not (0). The lock is released on every return after it was taken.

name: ossl_quic_conn_poll_events
prose: Reports which of the requested poll events currently hold for a QUIC SSL object (connection, stream or listener). Precondition: ssl is a QUIC object (else it returns 0 and p_revents is not written); events is a mask of SSL_POLL_EVENT_* bits; p_revents is non-NULL; the function takes the object lock itself. If the object has a connection that has not been started, only the writable event can be reported: SSL_POLL_EVENT_W is set in the result if it was requested, without testing any predicate, no reactor tick is performed even if do_tick is non-zero, and no other event is examined. Otherwise, if do_tick is non-zero it first runs one reactor tick. For an object with a stream component it then tests the read, read-exception, write and write-exception events requested. For a connection object (not a stream) it tests connection exception, connection exception drain, incoming bidirectional and unidirectional stream availability and outgoing bidirectional and unidirectional stream availability. For a listener it tests listener exception and incoming connection availability. Each bit is set only if it was requested and its test holds. It releases the lock, stores the resulting mask in *p_revents and returns 1.

name: qrx_process_pkt
prose: Processes one packet inside a received datagram: decodes the header, removes header protection, decrypts the body and queues the decrypted packet on the pending list. Precondition: pkt is a PACKET positioned at the start of this packet, pkt_idx is its index in the datagram, urxe is the datagram entry, first_dcid is the destination connection id of the first packet (used for coalesced packets), datagram_len is the full datagram length. Return value: 1 means the packet is deferred (its encryption level is not yet available, or 1-RTT is not yet allowed), after advancing pkt past this packet; 0 means the packet was either queued successfully or dropped as malformed, and the two cases are not distinguished by the return value. Behaviour: a free receive entry is reserved (failure goes to the malformed path); a packet already marked processed, a header that does not decode, or a header failing the early validation is malformed. An unencrypted packet type (such as version negotiation) is copied into a reserved entry, marked processed and appended to the pending list without decryption (a failed reservation is malformed). For encrypted packets the encryption level must exist (otherwise deferral; an error from the level lookup is malformed); for Initial packets the token pointer is relocated after a buffer relocation; the header protection is removed if this has not been done and the header decoded again; the header is validated, an optional message callback is invoked, a buffer for the plaintext is reserved (failure sets the end-of-packet pointer to NULL and goes to the malformed path), the body is decrypted (failure is malformed), and late validation is run (failure is malformed). A 1-RTT packet whose key phase differs from the current epoch triggers a key update initiation. On success the packet is marked processed, the entry receives the decrypted data, key epoch, addresses and receive time, the largest packet number of its space is updated, and it is moved from the free list to the pending list. In the malformed path the packet is marked processed and, if the end of this packet is known, only this packet is skipped; if it is unknown (early allocation failure, undecodable header, or the plaintext-buffer reservation failure) the whole rest of the datagram is skipped.

name: ossl_quic_stream_map_notify_reset_recv_part
prose: Handles a received RESET_STREAM for the receive part of stream qs. Precondition: qsm and qs valid; app_error_code and final_size come from the frame. The result depends on the receive state. If the stream has no receive part (state NONE or any unrecognised state) it returns 0 (caller error). In the states RECV, SIZE_KNOWN and DATA_RECVD it returns 0 if a final size was already known and differs from final_size (the final size may not change); the caller therefore does not have to guarantee equality, it is checked here. Otherwise it moves the state to RESET_RECVD, records the peer reset error code, clears want_stop_sending, frees the receive stream buffer and sets it to NULL, calls ossl_quic_stream_map_update_state, and returns 1. In the states DATA_READ, RESET_RECVD and RESET_READ it ignores the frame and returns 1 without changing anything and without comparing final_size (such a frame may be a reordered or retransmitted one).

name: txp_generate_stream_related
prose: Generates the stream-related frames (STOP_SENDING, RESET_STREAM, MAX_STREAM_DATA and STREAM data) for the streams that need to send something, into the packet under construction. Precondition: txp, pkt valid; have_ack_eliciting and tmp_head non-NULL; the stream map iterator visits streams with pending work. For each stream it first clears the per-packet bookkeeping flags (sent_fc, sent_stop_sending, sent_reset_stream, blocked, new credit consumed). If a STOP_SENDING is wanted it begins a frame (failure returns 0), encodes it (if it does not fit the frame is rolled back, the stream is linked on the temporary list and the loop stops with result 1), commits (failure returns 0) and marks it sent. If a RESET_STREAM is wanted it requires the stream to be in the reset-sent state (else returns 0), gets the final size (a failure returns 0), encodes and commits the frame the same way (rollback, link and stop when it does not fit), marks it sent and computes the flow control credit consumed (returning 0 if the final size is below the stream send window mark). If the receive part is still receiving and a MAX_STREAM_DATA is needed it is encoded and committed in the same manner. If the stream has a send buffer and is not reset it calls txp_generate_stream_frames; a failure links the stream on the temporary list and returns 0, otherwise the consumed connection credit is added up and, when the packet is full, the stream is linked and the loop stops with result 1. At the end of each loop iteration that did not break out the stream is linked on the temporary list. Returns 1 if the loop finished or stopped because a frame did not fit; returns 0 on the allocation, assertion or encoding failures listed. The failures at the begin and commit steps return 0 before the current stream is linked on the temporary list, whereas a failure inside txp_generate_stream_frames links it first.

name: tls_post_encryption_processing_default
prose: Finishes the record packet after the payload was encrypted: accounts for encryption growth, adds the MAC for encrypt-then-MAC, closes the length field, reports the header to the message callback and finalises the packet. Precondition: thispkt holds the record header and the encrypted payload, thiswr describes the record, mac_size is the MAC size (0 if none). Every failing step raises a fatal internal-error alert (SSL_AD_INTERNAL_ERROR) and returns 0. First it reads the packet length origlen and requires that the allowed overhead covers the record length (assertion), that encryption did not shrink the data (origlen <= thiswr->length), and, if the record is longer than origlen, it allocates the extra bytes in the packet (this growth is not added to thiswr->length, which already contains it). If encrypt-then-MAC is in use and mac_size is non-zero, it allocates mac_size bytes, computes the MAC into them and adds mac_size to the record length. It then reads the packet length and closes the length sub-packet. If a message callback is set it reports the record header (and, for TLS 1.3 with encryption active, the inner content type) before the packet is finished. It then finishes the packet and adds the header length (5 bytes, or 13 for DTLS) to thiswr->length. Returns 1 on success.

name: tls_write_records
prose: Record layer write entry point: builds the records for numtempl templates and sends them. Precondition: no earlier pipe buffer is still pending (rl->nextwbuf is past the last pipe or the next buffer has nothing left); otherwise it raises a fatal internal-error alert (ERR_R_SHOULD_NOT_HAVE_BEEN_CALLED) and returns OSSL_RECORD_RETURN_FATAL. It then calls the protocol-specific write_records method to encrypt and frame the templates into the write buffers; if that fails it returns OSSL_RECORD_RETURN_FATAL (the method itself is responsible for raising any error; none is raised here). It sets nextwbuf to 0 and returns the result of tls_retry_write_records, which writes the buffers to the BIO one after another: OSSL_RECORD_RETURN_SUCCESS when all pipes were written (nextwbuf then equals numwpipes, it is not reset to 0), OSSL_RECORD_RETURN_RETRY when the BIO asks for a retry (the position is kept for the next call), OSSL_RECORD_RETURN_FATAL when the BIO write fails without a retry condition (only a system error is queued, no alert), when no BIO is set (SSL_R_BIO_NOT_SET alert), or when a copy of a moving application buffer cannot be allocated, or the value returned by the optional prepare_write_bio hook when that is not success.

name: tls_default_read_n
prose: Reads at least n bytes into the record layer read buffer from the underlying BIO (up to max bytes when read-ahead allows) and sets *readbytes to n on success. Precondition: rl has a read buffer; n > 0 (n == 0 returns OSSL_RECORD_RETURN_NON_FATAL_ERR); extend non-zero means the data continues the current packet; clearold == 1 allows moving the pending data to the start of the buffer. With extend == 0 it starts a new packet: if no bytes are buffered (left == 0) the buffer offset is reset to the aligned start, otherwise the packet starts at the current offset (so it is not necessarily aligned), and the packet pointer is set with length 0. A NULL packet pointer is a fatal internal error. If the packet is not at the aligned start and clearold == 1, the packet and the buffered bytes are moved to the aligned start. For DTLS, an extend request with nothing buffered returns NON_FATAL_ERR (a record header without body) and n is reduced to the buffered amount if that is smaller. If the buffer already holds at least n bytes it takes them (advancing packet_length and offset, reducing left) and returns SUCCESS. If n does not fit in the rest of the buffer it is a fatal internal error. Otherwise it loops reading from the previous BIO (rl->prev) or the main BIO: in TLS without read-ahead it reads at most n bytes, otherwise up to max (capped to the buffer space); a read that would block on the previous BIO frees it and continues with the main BIO; on a retry, end of file or other failure it stores the count already read in rb->left (so the partial bytes stay buffered), releases the buffer in TLS (not DTLS) mode if release-buffers is set and nothing is held, and returns RETRY, EOF or FATAL (no BIO set raises SSL_R_READ_BIO_NOT_SET); for DTLS it stops after one read at the amount received. After enough bytes arrive it updates offset, left and packet_length and returns SUCCESS.

name: ssl3_cbc_copy_mac
prose: Extracts the MAC from the end of a decrypted CBC record in constant time with respect to the (secret) padding length, returning either the real MAC or a random one. Precondition: *reclen is the record length already reduced by the padding that the caller removed (good is all-ones if the padding was valid and 0 otherwise); origreclen is the original record length, recdata the record; origreclen must be at least mac_size and mac_size at most EVP_MAX_MD_SIZE (checked, else return 0); mac and alloced must be non-NULL when block_size != 1 (checked, else 0). If mac_size is 0 it returns 0 when good is 0 and 1 otherwise, touching nothing else. Otherwise it reduces *reclen by mac_size. For block_size 1 (no padding) the MAC position is fixed: it sets *mac to point into recdata at the new *reclen, *alloced to 0 and returns 1. For block ciphers it draws a random MAC with RAND_bytes_ex (failure returns 0), allocates a mac_size output buffer into *mac (failure returns 0) and sets *alloced to 1; it then scans only the last 256+mac_size bytes of the original record (the MAC position can only vary within that window; the scan assumes the MAC start is not before the scan start, which is not checked here), copying the MAC bytes into a rotation buffer with constant-time masks, and rotates them into place so the output is the real MAC when good is set and the random MAC when it is not. Returns 1 on success. The caller owns *mac when *alloced is 1.

name: dtls1_read_bytes
prose: DTLS read entry point: returns data of the requested record type to the caller, and processes alerts, change-cipher-spec records, retransmissions and renegotiation attempts it meets on the way. Precondition: s is a DTLS SSL; type is 0 (any) or application data or handshake; peek only with application data; buf has room for len bytes; readbytes non-NULL. Return values: 1 with *readbytes = n when bytes were copied; 0 for end of connection (received close_notify or fatal alert, shutdown state) or a zero-length request; a negative value for errors (fatal alerts raised for most of them) or retry conditions (rwstate set to reading); handshake function results are passed through. It returns -1 for an invalid type or peek combination (internal error alert) and runs the handshake function first if the connection is still in init (a negative result is returned, 0 becomes -1). In a loop (label start) it handles timeouts (retry the loop, or -1 on error state), reads records from the record layer when none is pending (a failed read goes through dtls1_read_failed, may retry or return its result), resets the alert counter for non-alert data, buffers a record that arrives out of order before ChangeCipherSpec was processed, and returns 0 after releasing a record when the peer shutdown was already received. A record of the requested type (or CCS while a handshake read with recvd_type is requested) is rejected with an alert if it is application data during the first handshake; with len == 0 it returns 0 without consuming, releasing the record only when it is empty (so a non-empty record stays pending); otherwise it copies min(len, available) bytes to buf and releases the consumed bytes (with peek, only an empty record is released and nothing is consumed), then returns 1 after setting *readbytes, except that for SCTP, when a shutdown was received and no message waits, it returns 0 after the bytes were copied into buf without setting *readbytes. Alerts: a malformed alert raises an alert and returns -1; a warning alert is counted (too many gives an alert and -1), close_notify returns 0 (or an SCTP retry -1), no_renegotiation raises a handshake failure and returns -1, other warnings continue the loop; a fatal alert records it, raises a fatal error, marks shutdown received, drops the session and returns 0; an unknown level raises an alert and -1. After SSL_SENT_SHUTDOWN a record is dropped and 0 returned. Change-cipher-spec records are released and the loop continues. A handshake record when not in a handshake: records from another epoch or too short are dropped; a Finished message triggers retransmission handling and, without auto-retry and with no unprocessed data, a retry -1; any other handshake message restarts the handshake function (renegotiation), with the same retry rule, and then continues the loop. Other record types give an unexpected-record alert and -1 (application data while expected otherwise may set in_read_app_data to 2 and return -1).

name: ssl3_write_bytes
prose: SSL/TLS write entry point of the record layer: writes len bytes of buf as records of the given type, resuming a previous partial write if one is pending. Precondition: ssl is a connection; if a write was interrupted the caller retries with the same buffer pointer and a length not smaller than the amount already written (s->rlayer.wnum) and the pending amount. Returns 1 with *written set (the full length, or the part written if partial writes are enabled for application data), or -1 or another non-positive value from a callee on error or retry. It sets rwstate to SSL_NOTHING and reads the resumed offset tot from wnum. A length smaller than wnum or than wnum plus the pending total raises a fatal alert (SSL_R_BAD_LENGTH) and returns -1; in that case, and for an early-data length limit failure, wnum is left unchanged. After those checks it sets wnum to 0, so a later return of 0 or less from the handshake function (which is run when the connection is still in init, a negative value is returned, 0 becomes -1) leaves wnum at 0 and not restored for a retry. It then asks tls_write_check_pending whether a previous write must be retried; a negative result is returned, a positive result retries the pending records (a result of 0 or less stores tot in wnum and returns it), and the pending total is added to tot. If nothing was written yet it records the pending type and buffer. If tot equals len it returns 1. A pending alert is dispatched first (a failure stores tot in wnum and returns it). The maximum and split fragment sizes must be non-zero and consistent (else fatal internal error and -1). In a loop it asks the record layer for the number of pipes, splits the remaining data into one template per pipe (full split-sized fragments if enough data, otherwise an even split), and writes them with write_records; a result of 0 or less stores tot in wnum and is returned; success returns 1 when everything (or, for application data with partial write enabled, whatever was written) is done, setting *written, otherwise it continues with the remainder.

name: ssl3_read_bytes
prose: SSL/TLS read entry point of the record layer: returns data of the requested record type to the caller, and handles alerts, handshake records (including renegotiation), change-cipher-spec and early data on the way. Precondition: type is 0 (any), application data or handshake; peek is only allowed with application data; buf has room for len bytes; readbytes non-NULL. An invalid combination raises an internal-error alert and returns -1. Return values: 1 with *readbytes set when data was delivered, 0 on a clean end (close_notify, fatal alert, shutdown already received, or a zero-length request), and -1 or a callee result for errors and retry conditions. If a handshake read is requested and bytes of a handshake message are buffered in handshake_fragment, it copies up to len of them to buf, removes them from the fragment, sets *recvd_type and *readbytes = n (n is 0 when len is 0) and returns 1. If the connection is still in init outside the handshake function it runs the handshake function first (negative result returned, 0 becomes -1). Then, at label start, it reads records from the record layer when none is pending (a non-positive read result is returned), rejects a TLS 1.3 non-handshake record while a handshake fragment is buffered, resets the alert counter for non-alert data, rejects data between CCS and Finished, and returns 0 if the peer shutdown was already received. A record of the requested type (or CCS for a handshake read with recvd_type, below TLS 1.3) is rejected with an alert for application data during the first handshake or CCS arriving with a pending handshake fragment; with len == 0 it returns 0 without consuming, releasing the record only if it is empty; otherwise it copies data from consecutive records into buf (several records only for application data) until len is reached; without peek the copied bytes are released from the record layer, with peek they are not consumed (only empty records are released); it returns 1 with the total in *readbytes, or loops again if nothing was copied. Alerts: malformed alert gives an alert and -1; warning alerts (or TLS 1.3 user_canceled) are counted, too many gives -1; user_canceled in TLS 1.3 continues; close_notify sets the received-shutdown flag and returns 0; fatal alerts (and any TLS 1.3 alert) record the alert, raise a fatal error, drop the session and return 0; no_renegotiation raises a handshake failure and -1; other warnings continue; unknown levels give -1. After a sent shutdown a handshake record is released and the read retried or reported as retry, and application data gives an alert and -1. Handshake records are copied into handshake_fragment (and released) and the loop continues until the fragment is full (4 bytes); with at least 4 bytes buffered outside the handshake the handshake function is run (renegotiation), returning -1 for early data reading or when auto-retry is off and no data is pending (retry), and otherwise continuing. A CCS record at this point is an alert and -1; other types give an unexpected-record alert and -1, except application data while the state machine allows it (in_read_app_data set to 2, -1), or skipped early data (counted and released, then continue).

name: DEFINE_RUN_ONCE_STATIC(do_wsa_startup)
prose: Windows-only initialiser body (compiled under OPENSSL_SYS_WINDOWS) defined with DEFINE_RUN_ONCE_STATIC(do_wsa_startup); it takes no arguments. It calls WSAStartup requesting Winsock version 2.2 and returns 0 if that call fails (nothing is changed). On success it sets the static wsa_started flag to 1, registers ossl_wsa_cleanup with OPENSSL_atexit (the registration result is not checked) so that WSACleanup runs at exit, and returns 1. The function itself does no once-only protection: it is meant to be called through RUN_ONCE in ensure_wsa_startup (rio_notifier.c:54-57), which runs it at most once per process and returns the stored result on later calls; a direct call would call WSAStartup again and register another atexit handler.

name: ssl_cipher_get_evp
prose: Looks up the EVP cipher, digest, MAC key type and secret size, and compression method that correspond to the cipher of session s. Precondition: ctx is the SSL_CTX (used for fetches); s is a session whose cipher field s->cipher is read; enc, md, mac_pkey_type, mac_secret_size and comp are output pointers, of which enc and md are required unless only comp is wanted. Returns 0 if s->cipher is NULL. If comp is non-NULL it sets *comp to NULL and looks the session compression method up in the registered compression methods, storing the entry if found; if enc and md are both NULL it then returns 1. If either of enc or md is NULL at that point it returns 0. It then fetches the cipher (ssl_cipher_get_evp_cipher, failure returns 0) and the digest/MAC data (ssl_cipher_get_evp_md_mac; failure frees *enc and returns 0). If the result has a cipher and either a digest or an AEAD cipher and a valid MAC (AEAD, no mac_pkey_type pointer, or a defined MAC key type) then it returns 1, after possibly replacing the cipher and digest by a combined stitched implementation: this is skipped (return 1 unchanged) when encrypt-then-MAC is used or the session version is not TLS 1.0 or later TLS 1.x; otherwise for RC4-MD5, AES-128/256-SHA1 and AES-128/256-SHA256 it fetches the matching cbc-hmac cipher and, if found, frees the old cipher and digest, sets *enc to it and *md to NULL. In all other cases (cipher or digest missing, or no valid MAC) it returns 0.

name: SSL_add1_host
prose: Adds a reference host name (or an IP address) to the verification parameters of the connection s. Precondition: s is an SSL; host may be NULL. Returns 0 if the connection object cannot be obtained. If host is non-NULL and parses as an IP address (a2i_IPADDRESS), it is treated as an IP address: if an IP address was already set it raises ERR_R_PASSED_INVALID_ARGUMENT ("IP address was already set") and returns 0 (only one IP address is allowed), otherwise it returns the result of X509_VERIFY_PARAM_set1_ip_asc. Otherwise it returns the result of X509_VERIFY_PARAM_add1_host(param, host, 0), which in add mode does not clear the existing host list: for a NULL or empty host (or one that is only a trailing NUL) it changes nothing and returns 1; a name with an embedded NUL byte, or an allocation failure, returns 0; otherwise a copy of the name is appended to the host list and 1 is returned. Thus 1 does not always mean that something was added.

name: dane_tlsa_add
prose: Adds one TLSA (DANE) record to dane. Precondition: dane has DANE enabled (trecs non-NULL), data non-NULL with dlen bytes. Returns -1 with SSL_R_DANE_NOT_ENABLED if DANE is not enabled. Invalid input returns 0 with an error: a length that does not fit an int (SSL_R_DANE_TLSA_BAD_DATA_LENGTH), usage above DANETLS_USAGE_LAST, selector above DANETLS_SELECTOR_LAST, an unknown matching type (no digest registered for it), a digest-matching record whose data length differs from the digest size, or NULL data (SSL_R_DANE_TLSA_NULL_DATA). Allocation failures of the record or its copy of the data return -1 without an error raised here. For a full-data matching type (0) the data are validated and partly cached: for the certificate selector the data must decode to exactly one X.509 certificate with a usable public key (else SSL_R_DANE_TLSA_BAD_CERTIFICATE, return 0); for usages other than PKIX-TA and DANE-TA the certificate is then discarded; for those two usages it is appended to dane->certs (creating that stack if needed; failure raises ERR_R_CRYPTO_LIB and returns -1, with dane->certs possibly left allocated but empty); for the public key selector the data must decode to exactly one public key (else SSL_R_DANE_TLSA_BAD_PUBLIC_KEY, 0), which is kept in the record only for DANE-TA usage. The record is inserted into dane->trecs at the position that keeps the list sorted by descending usage, then descending selector, then descending digest order; if the insert fails the record is freed, ERR_R_CRYPTO_LIB is raised and -1 is returned, but a certificate already appended to dane->certs remains there. On success dane->umask gets the bit of the usage and the function returns 1.

name: SSL_CTX_ctrl
prose: Control function of an SSL_CTX: gets or sets context settings according to cmd, with larg and parg carrying the arguments. Special cases come first: for SSL_CTRL_SET_GROUPS_LIST with larg == 1 it returns tls1_set_groups_list(ctx, ..., parg) as a syntax check, whether or not ctx is NULL. If ctx is NULL, SSL_CTRL_SET_SIGALGS_LIST and SSL_CTRL_SET_CLIENT_SIGALGS_LIST return tls1_set_sigalgs_list as a syntax check and every other command returns 0. With a non-NULL ctx the return value depends on cmd: read-ahead, max cert list, session cache size and mode set commands return the previous value (max cert list and cache size return 0 and change nothing for negative larg); the matching get commands return the current value; SSL_CTRL_SESS_NUMBER returns the session count and the SESS_* statistics commands return the counters; SSL_CTRL_MODE sets and CLEAR_MODE clears mode bits and return the new mode; SET_MAX_SEND_FRAGMENT returns 0 unless 512 <= larg <= SSL3_RT_MAX_PLAIN_LENGTH, otherwise stores it (lowering split_send_fragment if needed) and returns 1; SET_SPLIT_SEND_FRAGMENT returns 0 if larg is 0 or above the max fragment, else stores it and returns 1; SET_MAX_PIPELINES returns 0 unless 1 <= larg <= SSL_MAX_PIPELINES; CERT_FLAGS sets and CLEAR_CERT_FLAGS clears certificate flags and return the new flags; SET_MIN/MAX_PROTO_VERSION return 1 only if the allowed-version check and ssl_set_version_bound succeed (else 0) and the GET variants return the bounds; SET_MSG_CALLBACK_ARG stores parg and returns 1. Any other cmd is passed, with larg and parg, to ctx->method->ssl_ctx_ctrl and its result returned, so parg is used for those commands.

name: SSL_do_handshake
prose: Performs or continues the TLS/DTLS/QUIC handshake on s. If s is a QUIC object it returns the result of ossl_quic_do_handshake(s) immediately. Returns -1 if the connection object cannot be obtained, and -1 with SSL_R_CONNECTION_TYPE_NOT_SET if no handshake function is set (SSL_set_connect_state or accept state was not called). Otherwise it calls the method renegotiate check and, only when the connection is in initialisation or before the handshake, runs the handshake: when the async mode is set and no async job is currently running it starts an async job running ssl_do_handshake_intern and uses the value returned by ssl_start_async_job (for example the job pause or error outcomes, which that function maps to a return value that was not read); otherwise it calls sc->handshake_func(s) directly and returns its result (1 on success, 0 on controlled failure, negative on error or retry). If the connection is neither in init nor before the handshake it does nothing and returns 1.

name: ssl_clear_bad_session
prose: Removes the session of connection s from the session cache when it should be treated as bad, and reports whether it asked for the removal. Precondition: s is a connection. If s->session is non-NULL, the SSL_SENT_SHUTDOWN flag is not set, and the connection is neither in the initialisation state nor in the before state, it calls SSL_CTX_remove_session(s->session_ctx, s->session) and returns 1. In every other case it does nothing and returns 0. The return value of SSL_CTX_remove_session is ignored, so a result of 1 means the removal was requested, not that a session was actually removed from the cache.

name: tls_construct_ctos_early_data
prose: Client-side construction of the TLS 1.3 early_data extension in the ClientHello, which also settles which PSK session the client will offer. Returns EXT_RETURN_FAIL after a fatal alert on every error, EXT_RETURN_NOT_SENT when early data is not to be offered, and EXT_RETURN_SENT after writing an empty early_data extension. First, if a PSK use-session callback is set it is called (with the handshake digest when a HelloRetryRequest is pending); a callback failure, or a returned PSK session whose version is not TLS 1.3, frees the returned session and fails with SSL_R_BAD_PSK. If no session came back and the older PSK client callback is set (non-OPENSSL_NO_PSK builds) it is called to obtain identity and key: a key longer than the maximum or an identity longer than the maximum fails, and a non-empty key becomes a new session using the TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 cipher (failures set the alert and return, wiping the key but not freeing the half-built session). It then replaces s->psksession by the obtained session (freeing the old one); only when a session exists, it also replaces psksession_id with a copy of the identity (an allocation failure sets the length to 0 and fails), so when there is no PSK session the old identity is left unchanged. If the state is not early-data connecting, or neither s->session nor the PSK session allows early data, it sets max_early_data to 0 and returns NOT_SENT. Otherwise it takes the session that allows early data (s->session preferred over the PSK session), copies its max_early_data, and fails with an alert if its SNI hostname differs from the connection one, if the ALPN protocol it selected is not offered, or if the extension cannot be written; on success it marks early_data as rejected-until-confirmed (early_data = REJECTED, early_data_ok = 1) and returns SENT.

name: read_state_machine
prose: Drives the handshake message reading state machine of a connection (client or server) through the header, body and post-processing states, returning SUB_STATE_FINISHED when the last message of the flight was read and processed, or SUB_STATE_ERROR when it cannot continue now. The selection of the transition, process, size-check and post-process functions depends on s->server. On first use it sets first_packet and clears the first-init flag. In the HEADER state it reads a message header (tls_get_message_header or dtls_get_message; a result of 0 returns SUB_STATE_ERROR leaving read_state unchanged, so a retry resumes at the same place, whether the failure was a retry or an error is determined by the callee), calls the info callback, runs the transition function for the message type (failure returns SUB_STATE_ERROR) and rejects a message larger than the allowed maximum with a fatal alert, then moves to the BODY state. In the BODY state it reads the message body (0 returns SUB_STATE_ERROR), builds a PACKET over it (failure: fatal alert, SUB_STATE_ERROR), resets init_num and calls the process function: MSG_PROCESS_ERROR returns SUB_STATE_ERROR after checking whether a fatal error was already raised; MSG_PROCESS_FINISHED_READING stops the DTLS timer and returns SUB_STATE_FINISHED; MSG_PROCESS_CONTINUE_PROCESSING moves to POST_PROCESS with work state WORK_MORE_A; any other result returns to HEADER. In POST_PROCESS it stores the result of post_process_message in read_state_work: an error (after check_fatal) or a still-pending WORK_MORE_A/B/C returns SUB_STATE_ERROR, so in the pending case the work state has already been advanced for the retry; WORK_FINISHED_CONTINUE returns to HEADER; WORK_FINISHED_SWAP or STOP stop the DTLS timer and return SUB_STATE_FINISHED. An unknown read_state raises an internal-error alert and returns SUB_STATE_ERROR. The function loops until one of these returns.

name: tls_process_server_hello
prose: Client-side processing of a ServerHello (or a TLS 1.3 HelloRetryRequest, which has the ServerHello layout). Returns MSG_PROCESS_CONTINUE_READING for a normal ServerHello, the result of tls_process_as_hello_retry_request (MSG_PROCESS_FINISHED_READING on success) for a HelloRetryRequest, and MSG_PROCESS_ERROR after a fatal alert for any failure; the temporary extension list is freed on the error and normal exits. It parses the version, then the 32-byte random: when the connection is at TLS 1.3, the version field is TLS 1.2 and the random equals the HelloRetryRequest magic value, it is a HRR (a second HRR is an unexpected message; the record protocol version is set), otherwise the random is stored as the server random. It then parses the session id (at most the maximum size), cipher suite bytes, compression byte and the length-prefixed extensions block with no trailing data (a missing extension block is allowed except for a HRR). For a non-HRR it collects the extensions and selects the protocol version (ssl_choose_client_version). For TLS 1.3 or a HRR the compression must be 0 and the returned session id must equal the one the client sent. A HRR sets the cipher suite and continues in the HRR handler. Otherwise it checks the extension contexts, sets hit to 0, and for TLS 1.3 parses the PSK extension first (only on a record boundary) while for earlier versions it applies the session-secret callback if set (failure is fatal) and sets hit when the returned non-empty session id matches the cached session. For a resumed session the session id context must match. For a new session, if the cached session has an id a miss is counted and a new session is started; the session version is set, and, for versions below TLS 1.3 only, the session id length and bytes are copied from the message (in TLS 1.3 the session id is not saved). Then the negotiated version must match the session version, the cipher suite is validated and set, the compression method is checked against the cached or allowed methods, all extensions are parsed, in DTLS-SCTP with a resumed session the SCTP authentication key is derived and installed, and for TLS 1.3 the key block and handshake traffic hash are set up and the handshake write (unless middlebox compatibility or early data is in use) and read cipher states are switched.

prose: Final checks after the server flight has been received (certificate, status, key exchange and done). Returns 1 on success and 0 on failure. It returns 0 if ssl3_check_cert_and_algorithm fails (the alert is raised there). If a certificate status type was requested and the context has an OCSP status callback, the callback is called: a result of 0 raises SSL_R_INVALID_STATUS_RESPONSE (bad certificate status response alert) and returns 0, a negative result raises SSL_R_OCSP_CALLBACK_FAILURE and returns 0, a positive result continues. In builds with certificate transparency support, only when a CT validation callback is set on the connection, ssl_validate_ct is run, and a validation failure returns 0 only if peer verification is requested (SSL_VERIFY_PEER set); with the callback NULL no CT validation is done, and with a validation failure but no SSL_VERIFY_PEER the function continues and returns 1.

name: ossl_statem_client13_write_transition
prose: Chooses the next handshake state when the TLS 1.3 client is writing messages. Returns WRITE_TRAN_CONTINUE after setting st->hand_state to the next state, WRITE_TRAN_FINISHED without changing the state (switch to reading), or WRITE_TRAN_ERROR after a fatal internal-error alert. By current state: TLS_ST_CR_CERT_REQ goes to the compressed-certificate or certificate state when post-handshake authentication was requested, otherwise it requires that a shutdown was already sent (else fatal error, WRITE_TRAN_ERROR) and goes to TLS_ST_OK; TLS_ST_CR_FINISHED records the read time and goes to PENDING_EARLY_DATA_END (early data write retry or finished writing), CW_CHANGE (middlebox compatibility, no HelloRetryRequest), CW_FINISHED (no certificate request), or the compressed certificate or certificate state; TLS_ST_PENDING_EARLY_DATA_END goes to CW_END_OF_EARLY_DATA if early data was accepted and end-of-early-data is used, else behaves like the next case; TLS_ST_CW_END_OF_EARLY_DATA and TLS_ST_CW_CHANGE go to CW_FINISHED, or the (compressed) certificate state when a certificate was requested; TLS_ST_CW_COMP_CERT and TLS_ST_CW_CERT go to CW_CERT_VRFY if a certificate was requested, else CW_FINISHED; TLS_ST_CW_CERT_VRFY goes to CW_FINISHED; TLS_ST_CR_KEY_UPDATE, TLS_ST_CW_KEY_UPDATE, TLS_ST_CR_SESSION_TICKET and TLS_ST_CW_FINISHED go to TLS_ST_OK; TLS_ST_OK goes to CW_KEY_UPDATE if a key update is pending, otherwise it returns WRITE_TRAN_FINISHED without changing the state. Any other state (this function has no case for TLS_ST_BEFORE, TLS_ST_CW_CLNT_HELLO or TLS_ST_EARLY_DATA) is a fatal internal error and returns WRITE_TRAN_ERROR.

name: ossl_statem_client_write_transition
prose: Chooses the next handshake state when the client is writing messages (TLS 1.2 and earlier, DTLS, and the start of a connection). If the connection is at TLS 1.3 it returns the result of ossl_statem_client13_write_transition. Otherwise it returns WRITE_TRAN_CONTINUE after changing hand_state, WRITE_TRAN_FINISHED with the state unchanged, or WRITE_TRAN_ERROR (unknown state: fatal internal-error alert). TLS_ST_OK without renegotiation returns FINISHED, and with renegotiation falls through to TLS_ST_BEFORE; TLS_ST_BEFORE goes to CW_CLNT_HELLO. TLS_ST_CW_CLNT_HELLO goes to CW_CHANGE (middlebox compatibility) or TLS_ST_EARLY_DATA when early data is being connected and it is not a QUIC handshake; in every other case (no early data, or a QUIC handshake) it records the write time and returns FINISHED. TLS_ST_CR_SRVR_HELLO goes to CW_CHANGE (middlebox compatibility and early data not finished writing) or CW_CLNT_HELLO (for a retried ClientHello); TLS_ST_EARLY_DATA records the write time and returns FINISHED; DTLS_ST_CR_HELLO_VERIFY_REQUEST goes to CW_CLNT_HELLO; TLS_ST_CR_SRVR_DONE goes to CW_CERT if a certificate was requested, else CW_KEY_EXCH; TLS_ST_CW_CERT goes to CW_KEY_EXCH; TLS_ST_CW_KEY_EXCH goes to CW_CERT_VRFY if a certificate was requested and certificate verify is not skipped, else CW_CHANGE; CW_CERT_VRFY goes to CW_CHANGE; CW_CHANGE goes to CW_CLNT_HELLO (pending HelloRetryRequest), TLS_ST_EARLY_DATA (early data connecting), CW_NEXT_PROTO (next protocol seen, not DTLS) or CW_FINISHED; CW_NEXT_PROTO goes to CW_FINISHED; TLS_ST_CW_FINISHED goes to TLS_ST_OK when the session was resumed, otherwise returns FINISHED with the state unchanged; TLS_ST_CR_FINISHED goes to CW_CHANGE for a resumed session, else TLS_ST_OK; TLS_ST_CR_HELLO_REQ goes to CW_CLNT_HELLO after a successful renegotiation check and handshake setup (setup failure returns ERROR), otherwise to TLS_ST_OK.

name: dtls1_set_handshake_header
prose: Starts a DTLS handshake message in the packet pkt for message type htype. Returns 1 on success and 0 if a packet write fails. For a ChangeCipherSpec (htype SSL3_MT_CHANGE_CIPHER_SPEC): it copies next_handshake_write_seq into handshake_write_seq, sets the stored message header for the CCS with that sequence number, and writes the single CCS type byte to pkt (failure returns 0); no handshake header space is allocated and no sub-packet is started. For any other message type: it records the message header fields for htype (length and fragment fields zero for now), reserves DTLS1_HM_HEADER_LENGTH bytes at the current position for the header, to be filled in later, and starts a sub-packet for the body; if the header allocation or the sub-packet start fails it returns 0, and if only the sub-packet start fails the header bytes have already been reserved in pkt.

name: tls_finish_handshake
prose: Completes the handshake: frees temporary buffers, resets handshake bookkeeping, updates session caches and statistics, and runs the handshake-done callback. Precondition: s is a connection at the end of a handshake; wst is unused; clearbufs says whether to free the init buffers; stop selects the return value. Returns WORK_ERROR (with an internal-error alert) if freeing the write BIO buffer fails; otherwise WORK_FINISHED_STOP when stop is non-zero, or WORK_FINISHED_CONTINUE when stop is zero. With clearbufs set it frees s->init_buf (except for DTLS without SCTP), frees the write BIO buffer and resets init_num. A TLS 1.3 client that had requested post-handshake authentication moves it to the extension-sent state. Only if the stored cleanuphand flag is set (a handshake, not a post-handshake message, was completed) it resets renegotiate, new_session, cleanuphand and ticket_expected, clears the key block, and: for a server (TLS below 1.3) updates the session cache, counts a good accept and sets handshake_func to ossl_statem_accept; for a client removes the session from the cache in TLS 1.3 when client caching is on (else updates the cache), counts a hit and a good connect, and sets handshake_func to ossl_statem_connect; in DTLS it also resets the handshake sequence numbers and clears the received buffer. It then clears the in-init state, calls the info callback with SSL_CB_HANDSHAKE_DONE when one is set and the handshake was just cleaned up, or the protocol is below TLS 1.3, or this is the first handshake. Finally, when stop is zero it sets the in-init state again and returns WORK_FINISHED_CONTINUE; when stop is non-zero the connection is left out of the init state and WORK_FINISHED_STOP is returned. The stop argument is not used to choose handshake_func.

name: tls_process_client_hello
prose: Parses a ClientHello message on the server into a CLIENTHELLO_MSG and collects its raw extensions, without choosing the protocol version or cipher (that is done later in tls_early_post_process_client_hello). Returns MSG_PROCESS_CONTINUE_PROCESSING on success with s->clienthello set to the new structure, MSG_PROCESS_ERROR (after a fatal alert, freeing the structure and its extension list) for malformed or inconsistent messages, and MSG_PROCESS_FINISHED_READING in two non-error cases. Renegotiation: if this is not the first handshake and renegotiation is not already in progress, a TLS 1.3 connection is an internal error; if renegotiation is not permitted by the options (or the client lacks secure renegotiation binding and unsafe legacy renegotiation is not allowed) it sends a warning alert no_renegotiation and returns MSG_PROCESS_FINISHED_READING (no fatal error); otherwise it sets renegotiate and new_session. It allocates the message (failure is fatal). For an SSLv2-format hello (only allowed in the first handshake and without a pending HelloRetryRequest) it parses the SSLv2 fields (cipher list, session id up to the maximum, challenge) and builds the random from the last up to 32 bytes of the challenge, with a single null compression method. For the normal format it reads the random, the session id, the DTLS cookie (and for DTLS with cookie exchange enabled and an empty cookie it frees the structure and returns MSG_PROCESS_FINISHED_READING so the cookie exchange proceeds), the cipher suites, the compression methods and an optional length-prefixed extensions block with nothing trailing. Length or format errors raise decode-error or illegal-parameter alerts. It copies the compression methods (bounded), collects the raw extensions of the ClientHello (failure returns MSG_PROCESS_ERROR) and stores the message in s->clienthello.

name: rsa_keygen_test
prose: ACVP test case id for RSA key generation with known auxiliary values. It takes the id-th entry of rsa_keygen_data and returns 1 if all steps succeed and 0 otherwise (each step is wrapped in a test assertion that reports the failure). It converts the test xp1, xp2, xp, xq1, xq2 and xq values to BIGNUMs and passes them to the key generation as test parameters built with OSSL_PARAM_BLD; the public exponent is not part of these parameters: it is converted separately and set on the key generation context with EVP_PKEY_CTX_set1_rsa_keygen_pubexp, together with the modulus size. It creates an RSA key generation context, initialises it, applies the parameters and generates the key, then reads back p1, p2, q1, q2, the factors p and q, n and d as byte strings and compares each against the expected values of the test entry (a mismatch fails). On success it prints the values with test_output_memory. All temporaries (BIGNUMs, byte buffers, key, context, parameter list and builder) are released on every exit path after they were allocated.

name: setup_tests
prose: Test registration function of the ASN.1 time tests. It takes no arguments and registers test cases with the test framework through ADD_ALL_TESTS and ADD_TEST (the underlying add_test and add_all_tests functions return void, so there is no registration failure value to check) and then returns 1. It first probes whether time_t is signed and usable with negative values (localtime of -1 non-NULL and time_t not unsigned). It always registers the positive-value table test, the comparison table test, the duplicate test, the ASN.1-to-time_t conversion test and the tm-to-ASN.1 conversion test; it registers the negative-value table test only if negative time_t values are usable; it registers the 64-bit table test when time_t is wider than 32 bits, and in that case also the negative 64-bit table test when negative values are usable and the platform is not HP-UX. A log line is printed when the negative or 64-bit groups are added.

name: setup
prose: Command-line processing for the BIO prefix filter test program; returns 1 if all options were handled and 0 on any error (after printing a message for most errors). It creates text-mode BIOs on stdin, stdout and stderr (asserting that each exists) and then iterates over the options. -n AMOUNT sets the number of prefix filters from a decimal number (trailing characters give an error message and 0; an amount below 1 is rejected) and builds the filter chain with setup_bio_chain (failure prints a message and returns 0). -i [INDEX:]INDENT requires that the chain exists (the -n option came first), parses an optional filter index and the indent value in decimal, rejects an index not below amount, and sets the indentation of that filter with BIO_set_indent (failure returns 0). -p [INDEX:]PREFIX requires the chain, parses an optional index, checks it against amount and sets the prefix string of that filter with BIO_set_prefix (failure returns 0). Any other option, including the error option, returns 0 without a message from this function. The numbers are read with strtoul, which accepts leading white space and a sign, and an empty string is accepted as 0 because the check only looks for trailing characters. If setup_bio_chain fails after it freed the chain, the global chain pointer is not reset, so a later cleanup would free it again.

name: DEFINE_SET_GET_BASE_TEST(PREFIX, SETN, GETN, DUP, FIELD, TYPE, ERR, DEFAULT, NEW, FREE)
prose: Generated test function execute_CTX_<SETN>_<GETN>_<FIELD>(fixture) (from DEFINE_SET_GET_BASE_TEST, cmp_ctx_test.c:357-490) that exercises one setter and getter pair of a CMP context field. It returns 1 only if every check passed (TEST_true(res)), otherwise 0, and it reports each failed check with an error message. It requires that there is no pending error at the start and end. For an exported setter (PREFIX 1) the setter must return an error and queue an error when called with a NULL context; the getter must return the value ERR and queue an error for a NULL context. On the fixture context: the first get must return the default value; the setter is called with a first newly created value; a set0-style setter (SETN 0) takes ownership of it, so that value is not freed by the test afterwards, while a set1-style setter makes a copy; a get1-style getter (GETN 1) returns a value the test must free. After the first set the getter result must equal the stored pointer for SETN 0, or be a non-default value (and a different pointer when DUP is set) for SETN 1. The same is done with a second value, checking that the second set did not reset to the default, matches or copies as appropriate, differs from the first, and for GETN 1 returns a fresh object; a third get must be non-default and consistent (same pointer for GETN 0, a new copy when DUP is set for GETN 1). At the end it frees the values it still owns: the test-created values only when the setter did not take ownership (SETN != 0), and the values returned by get1 getters.

name: setup_tests
prose: Test setup for the configuration include tests. It returns 0 if any setup step fails and 1 after registering the tests. It creates a new NCONF object in the global conf (failure returns 0). It then processes the command-line options: the failure option sets expect_failure; the provider-test option sets test_providers (and then falls through to the next label, doing nothing more); the test-cases option does nothing; any other option returns 0. It takes the first non-option argument as the configuration file name and opens it into the global in BIO (a missing argument or an open failure returns 0 after a note). It then changes directory to the file location with change_path because the configuration files use relative names (failure returns 0), and registers the tests test_load_config, test_check_null_numbers and test_check_overflow, plus test_available_providers only when the provider option was given. ADD_TEST expands to a call of add_test, which returns void, so there is no registration failure that could make the function return 0 at this point.

name: are_ec_nids_compatible
prose: Decides whether two EC curve NIDs name the same curve, where some curves have two equivalent NIDs (the SEC name and the WAP WTLS name). Takes two int NIDs and returns 1 if they are compatible and 0 otherwise; it reads no global state. The result is computed by switching on n1d: for each curve with an alias pair (sect113r1/wtls4, sect163k1/wtls3, sect233k1/wtls10, sect233r1/wtls11, X9.62 c2pnb163v1/wtls5, which exist only when binary-field curves are not disabled, and secp112r1/wtls6, secp160r2/wtls7) it returns 1 when n2d is either member of the pair, whichever member n1d is. For secp224r1/wtls12 the result depends on the build: when the optimised NIST P curves are disabled (OPENSSL_NO_EC_NISTP_64_GCC_128 defined) the pair is symmetric like the others; otherwise only n1d == NID_wap_wsg_idm_ecid_wtls12 is special-cased, and it is compatible only with NID_secp224r1, while n1d == NID_secp224r1 goes to the default case and is compatible only with itself, so the relation is not symmetric there. For every other n1d (the default case) it returns 1 only when n1d == n2d.

Round-15 reviewer right: with OPENSSL_NO_EC_NISTP_64_GCC_128 defined n1d == NID_secp224r1 also accepts wtls12 (1772-1774), otherwise it goes to the equality default (1786-1787). No contract given since the result depends on build macros.
